overview: Syphax ruled the Masaesyles in western and central North Africa during the late third century BCE. His reign ended in 203 BCE, before this record’s imported 200 to 100 BCE map interval. The outline cannot establish his kingdom’s dates or precise borders.

periods.title: The historically documented king
periods.summary: Syphax appears in events around 220 BCE; the beginning of his reign remains unknown.

items.text: Siga in the west and Cirta farther east were royal centers. Syphax’s expanding kingdom brought different communities under one ruler, but its southern boundary remains uncertain.

Livy describes Syphax asking a Roman envoy to remain as an infantry instructor. Training meant organizing recruits and teaching them to keep formation: an army needed practice as well as horses and weapons.

In Appian’s account, Syphax hosted the rival commanders Scipio and Hasdrubal at a banquet, where they shared a dining couch. That is one way to make awkward dinner guests sit together. The story reflects the king’s importance to both powers.
Syphax married Sophonisba, daughter of the Carthaginian commander Hasdrubal, as their alliance strengthened. Royal family relationships and territorial competition were intertwined with the war.

sections.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings

items.text: Excavations beside the Tafna at Siga found successive buildings and thick layers of broken pottery. The excavator placed this occupation broadly across the Hellenistic centuries, beginning before Syphax. His capital had an existing urban past.

The Siga deposits included Campanian pottery and several amphora forms. These durable fragments give archaeologists evidence of containers and connections that survive when the people who handled them left no personal diary.

Builders at Siga strengthened walls with dressed stone. Vuillemot suggested that one room had a sloping earthen roof waterproofed with lime, but could not decide whether these large rooms were homes or storerooms. Archaeology sometimes leaves the room labels blank.

The nearby Beni Rhénane royal mausoleum illustrates regional building skill, although its date and royal owner are disputed. Craftspeople used stone from a nearby quarry and mortar incorporating local volcanic material and gypsum from the surrounding district.

At Beni Rhénane, underground chambers followed the monument’s curved and straight sides. Stone barriers closed entrances. These remains reveal specialized stoneworking and careful planning in the region’s royal funerary tradition.

sections.title: A king’s image and a written name

items.text: A surviving copper coin cataloged as Syphax’s measures 25 millimeters across and weighs 7.38 grams. The small object carries a bearded royal portrait on one side and a galloping rider on the other.

The rider’s cloak streams behind him and he holds a scepter; the king’s portrait wears a diadem. Those carefully chosen details turn a small piece of money into a portable statement of royal authority.

The coin’s Punic writing includes “SPQ”, the consonants of the name Syphax in scholarly transliteration. The longer legend adds a royal title. This is a written sample from his coinage, shown in Latin letters rather than a reconstruction of the original engraved shapes.

ending.text: Syphax lost his kingdom in 203 BCE and died in captivity in Italy. His son Vermina retained a reduced kingdom for a time, while Massinissa gained the eastern conquests. Numidian communities continued under new rulers.
